title: Tries & String Algorithms
summary: Store a million words so prefix lookups are instant, and find a needle in a haystack of text without re-reading the same characters twice.

blocks.markdown:
A **trie** is a tree where each edge is a character and each root-to-node path spells a word, so shared prefixes share nodes.

- Insert and search cost **O(L)** — L is the word length, independent of how many words you store.
- Killer use: **autocomplete** and prefix queries. Walk to the prefix node, collect everything below.
- The cost is **memory**: a node may reserve a slot per possible next character.
- Substring search is a separate problem — **KMP** and **Rabin–Karp** find a pattern inside text without re-reading characters.

blocks.subTitle: Which tool for which job
blocks.markdown:
Match the structure to the question you must answer.

| Need | Reach for |
|---|---|
| Autocomplete, prefix lookups | Trie |
| One pattern in one text | KMP |
| Many patterns, duplicate blocks | Rabin–Karp |
| Exact membership, no prefixes | Hash set |

If you never query a prefix, a hash set ([hashing](hashing)) is smaller and simpler.

blocks.subTitle: The trie structure
blocks.markdown:
Each node holds a map of **children** keyed by character and an **isEnd** flag marking where a word terminates. The root is the empty string.

![Trie storing cat, car, can, dog](assets/tries-string-algorithms/trie-structure.svg)

- "cat", "car", "can" share the `c→a` path and only fork at the third letter; "dog" sits on its own branch.
- A node can be **both** an end-of-word and have children — that is why you need the flag, not just leaf detection.

assets.alt: Trie storing cat, car, can, dog

blocks.subTitle: Insert, search, prefix
blocks.markdown:
All three are the same walk: step one character at a time.

```python
def insert(root, word):
    node = root
    for ch in word:
        node = node.children.setdefault(ch, TrieNode())
    node.is_end = True

def search(root, word):        # exact word?
    node = walk(root, word)
    return node is not None and node.is_end

def starts_with(root, prefix): # any word with prefix?
    return walk(root, prefix) is not None
```

- **search** checks `is_end`; **starts_with** just needs the node to exist.
- All **O(L)** — one step per character, no scanning the word list.

blocks.subTitle: Autocomplete from a trie
blocks.markdown:
Prefix queries fall right out of the layout — that is the whole point of a trie.

- Walk to the prefix node in **O(L)**.
- **DFS its subtree**, emitting a word every time you hit an `isEnd`.
- For top-k by popularity, store a frequency on each end node and keep a [heaps-priority-queues](heaps-priority-queues) during the walk.
- A hash set can't do this — the hash of `ca` tells you nothing about the hash of `cat`.

blocks.subTitle: KMP: the failure function
blocks.markdown:
KMP precomputes **lps[i]** — the longest proper prefix of `pattern[0..i]` that is also a suffix.

![KMP failure function for ABABC](assets/tries-string-algorithms/kmp-failure-table.svg)

- On a mismatch after matching `j` chars, set `j = lps[j-1]` instead of resetting to 0.
- Crucially the **text pointer never moves backward** — only the pattern slides.
- For "ABABC", `lps[3] = 2` because "ABAB" has "AB" as both a prefix and a suffix.
- Build is **O(m)**, search **O(n)**, total **O(n+m)**.

blocks.subTitle: Rabin–Karp: the rolling hash
blocks.markdown:
Treat each window as a number; comparing the window to the pattern becomes integer equality.

```python
def rabin_karp(text, pattern, B=256, M=1_000_000_007):
    m = len(pattern)
    high = pow(B, m - 1, M)
    hp = ht = 0
    for ch in pattern: hp = (hp * B + ord(ch)) % M
    for ch in text[:m]: ht = (ht * B + ord(ch)) % M
    for i in range(len(text) - m + 1):
        if ht == hp and text[i:i+m] == pattern:  # verify!
            yield i
        if i < len(text) - m:
            ht = ((ht - ord(text[i]) * high) * B + ord(text[i+m])) % M
```

- Each **roll** is O(1): drop the left char, add the new right char.
- Always **verify** on a hash match — hashes collide.

blocks.subTitle: KMP vs Rabin–Karp vs naive
blocks.markdown:
All find a pattern in text — they guarantee different things.

| Aspect | KMP | Rabin–Karp |
|---|---|---|
| Time | O(n+m) always | O(n+m) average |
| Worst case | O(n+m) | O(n·m) |
| Best at | One pattern | Many patterns |

- **Naive** is O(n·m); fine for tiny inputs and readable.
- KMP gives a **hard linear guarantee** even on hostile input.
- Rabin–Karp shines for **many needles** or comparing many fixed-length blocks.

blocks.subTitle: Trie vs hash set, and saving memory
blocks.markdown:
A trie is not automatically better than a hash set.

- **Exact membership only** → hash set; O(1) lookup, far less memory.
- **Prefix queries** → trie; nothing else answers them cleanly.
- **Large alphabet** → use a hash-map-backed node, not a fixed array per node.
- **Long single-child chains** → a **radix / compressed trie** merges them into one edge to save space.

blocks.subTitle: Real systems
blocks.markdown:
These algorithms run inside the tools you use daily.

- **Search engines** — Lucene stores its term dictionary in an **FST**, a compressed trie cousin, so type-ahead and prefix queries stay fast ([search-indexing](search-indexing)).
- **IP routers** — longest-prefix match uses a **radix/PATRICIA trie** over address bits; a hash can't do "longest prefix".
- **rsync & dedup** — a **rolling hash** spots shared blocks even when they shift position.
- **grep** — usually **Boyer–Moore**, which skips characters, beating textbook KMP on real text.

blocks.subTitle: Signals in production
blocks.markdown:
How these show up on dashboards:

- **Autocomplete p99 spikes** → dictionary no longer fits in memory, or subtree DFS isn't bounded by top-k.
- **Trie memory creep** → too many unique terms, or array nodes where a radix trie is needed; a sudden jump often means a new alphabet.
- **Rising Rabin–Karp verification-failure rate** → weak modulus or base, or too-small window; tune the hash.
- **Substring-scan CPU regression** → input started hitting the O(n·m) worst case; switch to a linear matcher.

The mistakes that bite in interviews and production:

- **"A trie always beats a hash set."** Only when you need prefixes; otherwise it just burns memory.
- **"Every node needs 26 pointers."** Only for hardcoded lowercase English — use a map or radix trie for big alphabets.
- **"KMP makes the pattern jump around the text."** Opposite: the **text** pointer never rewinds; the pattern slides via lps.
- **"lps is whether a prefix repeats."** It's the longest *proper* prefix that is *also a suffix* — both words load-bearing.
- **"Equal Rabin–Karp hashes mean equal strings."** Never — verify characters, or you report false matches.
